newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs celebrate Orthodox Christmas in Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Serbs celebrate Orthodox Christmas in Sarajevo.

text.p: Serbs celebrated Orthodox Christmas on Tuesday in an ancient church in the centre of Sarajevo, giving thanks for a year without war in Bosnia.
Some 200 mostly elderly people filled the Old Orthodox Church for the Christmas ceremony, lighting candles for the living and the dead.
Bosnia's Roman Catholic Cardinal Vinko Puljic, fufilling a Sarajevo tradition, visited the church during the service and greeted Orthodox Priests Dusan Jovanovic and Krstan Bjelac.

In Sarajevo, which has a population of about 380,000, the Serb community has dwindled to some 8,000 after a 3-1/2 year war that pitted the mainly Moslem Bosnian government against separatist Serb forces who laid siege to the capital.
"I feel wonderful this Christmas. There are no shells, no shooting and may God grant us peace," said Radmila Moric, 46, after the church service.
Moric said her son served in the Moslem-led Bosnian government army and that she had no intention of leaving Sarajevo. "My grandfather and grandmother were born here and I don't want to leave."
Sarajevo state television broadcast the Orthodox service and also aired Catholic Christmas mass last month.
Human rights workers say the Moslem-Croat Federation allows for more religous freedom than Bosnia's Serb Republic, which has virtually wiped out all traces of Islam on its territory.
The ultra-nationalist Serb leadership expelled Moslems and Roman Catholics from conquered land and blew up ancient mosques during the 1992-95 war.
Official Bosnian Serb television only recognises Orthodox Christian holidays and portrays Bosnian Moslems as fanatics.

A spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, appealed to Bosnian political leaders to drop hostile rhetoric and use language in keeping with the spirit of Christmas in the new year.
"The meaning of Orthodox Christmas is surely one of peace to all men and women of goodwill," Colum Murphy told a news conference.
"We should ask is this message this year an abstraction or a genuine sentiment...The language of peace building is, we think, very important."
